title: The missed Friday
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative; your unit’s emergency protocol and the team’s orders come first. No doses are given here on purpose.
intro: Rey Fernandez, 15 years old and 45 kilograms, is on hemodialysis through a tunneled catheter. He missed Friday’s session for a school event and arrives Monday at 7:00 a.m. He says his legs feel heavy and weak. His pulse is slow and irregular, and the monitor shows tall, peaked T waves. His potassium has just been sent.

choices.text: Keep him lying down on the monitor, call the nephrologist and emergency team, bring the cart.
choices.feedback: Weakness, a slow irregular pulse and peaked T waves after a missed session are life-threatening hyperkalemia until proven otherwise. The ECG justifies acting now.

choices.text: Wait for the potassium result, then call the nephrologist with the exact number and the ECG.
choices.feedback: The result confirms; it should not delay. Arrhythmias in hyperkalemia can be sudden.
choices.then: His pulse slows further. You call the team and bring the cart.

choices.text: Let him walk to the restroom and sit in the waiting area until his chair is ready.
choices.feedback: He needs continuous monitoring and must not be alone or walking. A collapse in the restroom is the outcome this step invites.
choices.then: A colleague brings him back on a wheelchair. You put him on the monitor and call the team.

n2.scene: The nephrologist and emergency team arrive and take the lead. They will give emergency treatment per the unit’s protocol.

choices.text: Take the role the leader assigns: prepare ordered medicines, read back, keep time.
choices.feedback: Clear roles and closed-loop communication make a resuscitation safer. The leader chooses the treatment; you make it happen accurately and on time. Per protocol; read back each order and keep the time record.

choices.text: Before the leader speaks, give a medicine from the cart on your own to save time.
choices.feedback: Uncoordinated drugs cause errors: wrong drug, wrong dose, doubled doses. Wait for the order and read it back.
choices.then: The leader stops you, assigns roles, and gives orders.

choices.text: Stay at the desk to finish the morning chart, since enough people are at the bedside.
choices.feedback: The team needs every pair of hands. Charting can wait; the time record is a role in the room.
choices.then: The leader calls you in to prepare medicines and keep time.

n3.scene: His potassium comes back high. After treatment, his rhythm is improving. The nephrologist orders urgent hemodialysis.

choices.text: Prepare urgent dialysis as ordered, with the monitor kept on throughout.
choices.feedback: Emergency treatment shifts potassium for a time; dialysis removes it. Release checks still apply in an emergency. Machine released, catheter assessed and hubs scrubbed, dialysate as ordered.

choices.text: The ECG looks better, so send him back to the waiting area until his usual slot.
choices.feedback: The shift is temporary. Without removal, potassium rises again.
choices.then: The nephrologist insists on urgent dialysis; you prepare it.

choices.text: Wait for a repeat potassium before preparing the machine, in case it was hemolyzed.
choices.feedback: A repeat may be ordered, but preparation can run in parallel; waiting adds avoidable delay.
choices.then: You prepare the machine while the repeat is drawn.

n4.scene: Rey’s mother arrives, frightened, asking what is happening and whether he will die.

choices.text: One team member stays with her, explains simply, and keeps her updated.
choices.feedback: Family support is a named role. A calm explanation helps her and keeps the bedside clear for the team. As the leader assigns.

choices.text: Ask her to leave the unit without explanation, so the team can work.
choices.feedback: She may need to step back from the bedside, but not without someone explaining and staying with her.
choices.then: You assign a colleague to sit with her and explain.

choices.text: Answer her questions yourself while also preparing medicines.
choices.feedback: Kind, but splitting attention during medicine preparation invites errors. Ask the leader to assign someone.
choices.then: The leader assigns a colleague to support her.

n5.scene: Rey is well. At his next session he says the school event “mattered more than one dialysis”.

choices.text: Talk privately, without lecturing; plan for school events with him; involve the social worker.
choices.feedback: Adolescents miss sessions for reasons. Partnership and a schedule that fits his life prevent the next emergency better than blame. About what happened and why; for example rescheduling a session around school events.

choices.text: Warn him in front of other patients that he could have died because he was irresponsible.
choices.feedback: Public shame breaks trust and makes the next missed session more likely, not less.
choices.then: You apologize and arrange a private conversation and a schedule plan.

choices.text: Write “noncompliant” in the chart and remind him of the rules next session.
choices.feedback: The label explains nothing and solves nothing. Find the reason and plan with him.
choices.then: You arrange a private conversation and a schedule plan.

end.title: Safe, with a plan
end.text: Rey’s potassium is back in range, and he has a schedule that lets him attend school events without missing dialysis. You record the times of recognition, the team call, treatment, the potassium, dialysis start, and the follow-up plan.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Act on the ECG. Symptoms, a slow irregular pulse and peaked T waves after a missed session are an emergency before the laboratory confirms it.
  • Roles and read-back. The leader orders; you prepare, read back and keep time.
  • Shift, then remove. Emergency treatment buys time; urgent dialysis removes the potassium.
  • Family support is a role.
  • Partnership prevents the next one. Find the reason for the missed session and plan with the adolescent.
